A run holds everything the workload is sized for from the moment it is placed; when it ends — stopped, exited, failed, or reported gone by the node — everything returns to the node. A run's end is recorded once, so a stop and the node's own report of the same end cannot return the room twice. A node that registers again rebuilds its free capacity from the workload records still running on it, so a run the node ended while the server was away is still accounted for; the write is conditional on the counters it overwrites, so a reservation or a release landing between the records' read and the write is answered by a rebuild run again on what is there.

The node keeps nothing of a run that has ended: once the server holds its outcome, the node removes the VM, its disk and its log files (after the shipper has read them). The workload's record stays on the server with its status and exit code, and its logs stay in the organization's log store under its id, until the record is deleted (see

The VMs are the same size in every environment; what differs between nodes is how many fit. The sync VM gets half a core, 2 GB of memory and a 2 GB root filesystem, where the package manager keeps its cache, with the project checkout mount (clone plus installs) capped at 4 GB; each runtime VM, and each site publish or removal VM and SBOM VM, gets half a core, 1 GB of memory and a 512 MB root filesystem — the checkout is a read-only mount, so the root holds only what the microservice writes. The disk caps are enforced where the node's filesystem carries project quotas.

A workload's record is the only link to its logs, so nothing deletes one as a side effect: destroying a workload removes its VM and its disk from the node and records the run
, and the record and its logs stay. Deleting a workload, from the console or through
, is the one way either goes: it deletes every log line the workload wrote from the organization's Loki tenant (the platform's own,

, for a platform workload), then the record, and refuses a run still open on its node — stop or destroy it first. The retention sweep, one cluster singleton beside the reconcile master, runs hourly and deletes the records of runs that ended longer ago than the retention period the same way, a page of a hundred at a time until none is left.

The Loki deletion API needs the compactor's retention and a delete request store, which

(the object store on Azure) configure, as does the compose file; without them a delete fails and the record stays for the next sweep. Loki's queriers filter a deleted range out of query results once they load the request, at their first query for the tenant or their five-minute reload, at a cost on every query in the tenant until its compactor applies the request, which the configured cancel period of one hour bounds; the sweep asks once per organization for every workload in a page, so a busy platform adds one pending request per organization per hour.

Trace logging prints every STOMP frame the gateway reads and writes, every service invocation the
invoker dispatches, and the arguments each invoked method received. That is what makes it useful
during development and what makes a high-frequency service — a heartbeat, a poll — drown out
everything else in the log.

Each entry is matched against the fully qualified CRI with Ant wildcards —

covers every method of a service and a raw CRI
covers just that one method. A scoped invocation carries its scope in the CRI, so a pattern that

An include wins over an exclude that also matches, which turns the filter around: exclude
everything and name what is worth watching.

Patterns are matched against every destination but one. A reply comes back on a destination
belonging to the client connection rather than naming what was invoked, so it is never matched —
an excluded request is marked as it enters the gateway and its reply is dropped from the log along
with it.
An excluded CRI therefore drops the whole exchange: the request frame, the invocation and its
arguments, the values a streaming result emits, and the reply frame the client receives. The
patterns are consulted only while trace logging is enabled, and cost nothing at any other level.
